opus-5.5.text:
Freeways matter a lot because of how people actually move around a metro area. If you look at cities like Phoenix, the San Francisco Bay Area, or Los Angeles, a huge share of trips, especially the longer and more valuable ones, use a freeway for at least part of the route. Airport runs are the classic example: getting from downtown San Francisco to SFO, or across Phoenix to Sky Harbor, is much faster on the highway. If you can only use surface streets, you either take a much slower route or you just can't serve that trip well, and riders notice. So freeway capability really unlocks the service: it makes trips faster, it extends the reach of the service area, and it makes Waymo a real option for the full range of things people use a car for, not just short hops around the city center.

From a technical side, freeways are interesting because in some ways they look simpler. The roads are structured, there are no pedestrians at crosswalks, no cyclists weaving through intersections. But the speeds are much higher, so the margin for error shrinks and the consequences of rare events are bigger. You have to handle things like debris on the road, stalled vehicles, construction zones that change the lane geometry, aggressive merges, and emergency vehicles, and you have to perceive and react at longer ranges. The long tail looks different from the city's long tail, and you have to validate that you're handling it safely before you remove the safety driver. That's why we took a deliberate path, with employee-only operation first and lots of simulation and validation, before opening it up to riders.

Ultimately it's about delivering a product people can rely on for their daily lives. If the car can take you anywhere you'd want to go in a region, the way a human driver would, including the freeway, that's when autonomous ride-hailing goes from a novelty to something that actually replaces how you get around.

r001.rationale: The response says freeway routes make trips faster and gives an across-Phoenix airport example, but it does not clearly say this shortens trips across Waymo’s geographically extensive Phoenix service area. Its reference to extending the service area describes freeway access expanding coverage.

fable-5.1.text:
Freeways are really where a lot of the value is for riders. If you think about how people actually move around a metro area, a big fraction of the longer trips, the airport runs, the commute across town, the trip from one neighborhood to another, naturally route onto the freeway. If you can't drive the freeway, you end up taking surface streets, and that can turn a twenty-minute trip into forty or fifty minutes. So from a customer standpoint, it's about time. It makes the service feel like a real alternative to driving yourself or taking a rideshare, rather than something that only works for short hops downtown.

It also unlocks the geography. Once you can connect the places you serve via freeways, the effective service area grows a lot without having to densely map and validate every single surface street in between. Things like airport trips become practical, which is one of the most requested use cases we hear about.

And then there's the technical side, which is why it took us a while. Freeway driving looks simpler in some ways, since there are no pedestrians or intersections, but the speeds are much higher. That means your perception range needs to be longer, your prediction has to be reliable farther out, and the consequences of a mistake are more severe. You also have to handle things like merging, lane changes with fast-moving traffic, debris on the road, and what to do if the vehicle has an issue and needs to pull over safely at seventy miles an hour. We spent a long time testing with safety drivers, then with employees, before we felt confident opening it up fully driverless. So it's important both because riders want it and because doing it well is a meaningful milestone for the capability of the system as a whole.

r001.rationale: The response says freeway access can shorten trips and expand the effective service area, but it does not identify Phoenix or explain the benefit across Waymo’s geographically extensive Phoenix service area.

astra-6.text: Freeways are a really important part of how people get around. If you want to take a longer trip across a city, or get to the airport, avoiding the freeway can add a lot of time. So for our customers, fully driverless freeway travel means more direct routes, shorter trips, and access to more destinations. It’s a key part of making the service useful for their everyday transportation needs.

r001.rationale: The response says freeway travel can make trips shorter and routes more direct, but it does not connect this benefit to Waymo’s geographically extensive Phoenix service area.

sol-6.1.text:
Freeways are really important because they connect so many of the places our riders want to go. If you can’t take the freeway, you may have to take a much longer route on surface streets. So enabling fully driverless freeway travel makes the service more useful—it can shorten trips and allow us to serve more destinations efficiently.

From a technical perspective, it also brings a different set of challenges. You’re operating at higher speeds, you need to merge and change lanes smoothly, and you need to handle things like construction and vehicles stopped on the shoulder. Being able to do that safely is an important step toward giving customers a service they can rely on for more of their everyday travel.

r001.rationale: The response says freeway access can shorten trips, but it does not connect that benefit to Waymo’s geographically extensive Phoenix service area.
